position: both — *unsafe working conditions*, *The bridge is unsafe*

senses.gloss: Likely to cause harm, or not protected from harm.
examples: The inspector closed the plant after finding *unsafe* conditions.
The water here is *unsafe* to drink.
She felt *unsafe* walking home after dark.

position: predicative only — after *leave*, *go* or *remain*: *left unsaid*, *what went unsaid*
contrast: Not the same as *unspoken*. An *unspoken* rule is understood without being stated; something *unsaid* was simply never said, often on purpose: *Some things are better left unsaid*.

senses.gloss: Not said, though it could have been.
examples: Some things are better left *unsaid*.
A lot went *unsaid* at dinner that night.
The apology remained *unsaid* for twenty years.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unsalted butter*

senses.gloss: Made or cooked without salt added.
examples: The recipe calls for a stick of *unsalted* butter.
We buy *unsalted* nuts for the kids.
These crackers are completely *unsalted*.

contrast: American writing uses *unsanitary*; the British word for the same thing is *insanitary*.

senses.gloss: Dirty enough to be a danger to health.
examples: The restaurant was shut down for *unsanitary* conditions.
Workers were living in crowded, *unsanitary* housing.
Storing raw meat that way is *unsanitary*.

contrast: Three neighbors that learners mix up: a result is *unsatisfactory* (not good enough), a person is *unsatisfied* (not pleased), and an experience is *unsatisfying* (it leaves you wanting more).

senses.gloss: Not good enough for what is needed.
examples: His explanation was *unsatisfactory*, so we asked again.
The company gave us an *unsatisfactory* answer about the delay.
Two students received an *unsatisfactory* grade in the course.

senses.gloss: Not pleased, because something fell short of what you wanted.
examples: Customers who are *unsatisfied* can return the item for a refund.
She left the meeting *unsatisfied* with the answers.
He was *unsatisfied* even after a second helping.

senses.gloss: Not met or filled, said of a need, a demand or a condition.
examples: There is still a large *unsatisfied* demand for affordable housing.
The loan will not close while two conditions remain *unsatisfied*.

position: both — *an unsatisfying job*, *The ending was unsatisfying*
contrast: The *-ing* word describes the thing (*an unsatisfying movie*); the *-ed* word describes the person (*I was unsatisfied*).

senses.gloss: Leaving you wanting more; not giving a feeling of satisfaction.
senses.ru: не приносящий удовлетворения, оставляющий чувство незавершённости
examples: The movie had a rushed, *unsatisfying* ending.
A salad alone makes for an *unsatisfying* lunch.
After ten years the work had become *unsatisfying*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unsaturated fats*

senses.gloss: Of a fat or oil, having double bonds between carbon atoms, and so generally better for your health.
examples: Olive oil is high in *unsaturated* fat.
The label lists both *unsaturated* and saturated fats.
Most of the fat in walnuts is *unsaturated*.

senses.gloss: Not yet stored on a computer, so it can be lost.
examples: A warning popped up about *unsaved* changes.
The laptop died and an hour of *unsaved* work went with it.
The draft is still *unsaved*, so do not close the tab.

contrast: American spelling is *unsavory*; British books print *unsavoury*. The usual meaning today is moral, not about food.

senses.gloss: Morally unpleasant; the kind of person or business you would not want to be seen with.
examples: He got mixed up with some *unsavory* characters downtown.
The report revealed *unsavory* details about the company.
The bar has an *unsavory* reputation.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant to taste or smell.
examples: The stew was gray and frankly *unsavory*.
An *unsavory* smell came from the refrigerator.

contrast: It almost never stands before a noun. Say *He walked away unscathed*, not *an unscathed man*.

senses.gloss: Not hurt or damaged at all by something dangerous.
examples: Both drivers walked away *unscathed*.
The old church came through the fire *unscathed*.
Her career emerged *unscathed* from the scandal.

senses.gloss: Not planned in advance, and not on the official schedule.
examples: The plane made an *unscheduled* landing in Denver.
We had an *unscheduled* visit from the fire marshal.
An *unscheduled* power outage shut the lab for a day.

senses.gloss: Not following the methods of science; not based on evidence.
examples: My survey of six friends was thoroughly *unscientific*.
The claim rests on *unscientific* reasoning.
Testing one sample is an *unscientific* way to decide.

senses.gloss: Not written or rehearsed in advance.
examples: The best part of the show was an *unscripted* moment with the audience.
He gave an *unscripted* answer that made headlines.
Their conversation felt completely *unscripted*.

senses.gloss: Willing to cheat or hurt people to get what you want.
examples: *Unscrupulous* landlords take advantage of new arrivals.
The fund was run by an *unscrupulous* broker.
He is ambitious but not *unscrupulous*.

senses.gloss: Not closed tightly, or no longer kept closed.
examples: The envelope arrived *unsealed*.
Do not store flour in an *unsealed* container.
The court records were *unsealed* last week.

ru: не по сезону, несвойственный времени года
position: both — mostly before a noun: *unseasonable warmth*
contrast: The adverb *unseasonably* is far more common than the adjective: *unseasonably warm for October*. Do not confuse it with *unseasoned*, which is about food without salt or spices.

senses.gloss: Not the weather you expect at that time of year.
examples: We got *unseasonable* heat in early April.
An *unseasonable* frost killed the young plants.
The rain was heavy and quite *unseasonable*.

position: both — the 'inexperienced' sense goes before a noun

senses.gloss: Cooked without salt, pepper or other flavorings.
examples: Plain *unseasoned* chicken tastes like cardboard.
The rice came to the table *unseasoned*.

senses.gloss: Without experience in a job, especially compared with older colleagues.
examples: The team started an *unseasoned* rookie at quarterback.
An *unseasoned* manager might have panicked.

senses.gloss: Of a loan or debt, not backed by property the lender can take.
examples: Credit card debt is *unsecured*, so the rate is higher.
The bank offers small *unsecured* loans to new customers.

senses.gloss: Not locked, fastened or protected.
examples: Never log in to your bank on an *unsecured* network.
The ladder was left *unsecured* in the back of the truck.

contrast: A sports word. In tennis the top players are ranked, or *seeded*, before a tournament; everyone else is *unseeded*.

senses.gloss: Not given a ranking in a tournament draw.
examples: An *unseeded* teenager beat the defending champion.
She went into the tournament *unseeded*.
Two *unseeded* players reached the semifinals.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an unseemly argument*
contrast: The *-ly* ending makes it look like an adverb, but it is an adjective. Say *He behaved in an unseemly way*, not *He behaved unseemly*.

senses.gloss: Not proper for the occasion, in a way that embarrasses people.
examples: There was an *unseemly* scramble for the last seats.
Arguing over money at a funeral is *unseemly*.
The senator called the remark *unseemly* and beneath the office.

position: both — also after the noun: *forces unseen*
contrast: *Sight unseen* is a fixed phrase meaning without looking at the thing first: *He bought the car sight unseen*.

senses.gloss: Not seen or noticed by anyone.
examples: She slipped out the back door *unseen*.
An *unseen* hand seems to be guiding the market.
The museum is showing previously *unseen* photographs.

senses.gloss: Putting other people first instead of yourself.
examples: It was an *unselfish* decision to give up the room.
The point guard is famous for *unselfish* passing.
She is the most *unselfish* person I know.

senses.gloss: Written or prepared but never sent.
examples: She kept a folder of *unsent* letters to her father.
The email sat *unsent* in my drafts for a week.
He found an *unsent* text on her phone.

senses.gloss: Looking at things plainly, without letting feelings soften the picture.
examples: The book gives an *unsentimental* account of the war.
She was *unsentimental* about selling the old house.
He has an *unsentimental* view of what the team needs.

senses.gloss: Not decided or finished.
examples: The question of who pays is still *unsettled*.
Several claims remain *unsettled* after two years.
The law in this area is *unsettled*.

senses.gloss: Uneasy and worried, unable to relax.
examples: The news left me *unsettled* all afternoon.
The baby was *unsettled* after the long flight.

senses.gloss: Of weather, likely to change and turn bad.
examples: The forecast calls for *unsettled* weather through the weekend.
Conditions stayed *unsettled* until Thursday.

senses.gloss: Dull, not exciting, and so easy to ignore.
examples: Maintenance is the *unsexy* part of the job that keeps everything running.
It is an *unsexy* topic, but it decides the budget.
Reliable and boring beats exciting and broken, however *unsexy* that sounds.

senses.gloss: Not physically attractive.
examples: He complained that the uniform was deeply *unsexy*.
There is nothing *unsexy* about confidence.

senses.gloss: Freed from something that was holding you back.
examples: *Unshackled* from the old contract, the band recorded whatever it wanted.
Critics warned about an *unshackled* presidency.
He played like a man *unshackled*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unshakable faith*
contrast: Also spelled *unshakeable*; American writing prefers *unshakable*. It describes beliefs and feelings, not physical objects.

senses.gloss: So firm that nothing can change it.
examples: She has an *unshakable* belief in her students.
His confidence at the plate is *unshakable*.
The two men formed an *unshakable* friendship.

contrast: *Unshaken* says that something did not change under pressure; *unshakable* says that nothing ever could.

senses.gloss: Still as firm as before, in spite of what happened.
examples: Her faith in him was *unshaken*.
The coach seemed *unshaken* by the loss.
Support for the plan remains *unshaken*.

senses.gloss: Not having shaved, so the face looks rough.
examples: He came to the door *unshaven* and half asleep.
An *unshaven* man in a gray coat was waiting outside.
She liked him better *unshaven*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unsightly stains*
contrast: Another *-ly* adjective, never an adverb. It is about how something looks, not about eyesight.

senses.gloss: Ugly to look at.
examples: An *unsightly* pile of trash had built up behind the store.
The cream is supposed to hide *unsightly* scars.
The new fence is frankly *unsightly*.

senses.gloss: Without a signature, and so not yet valid.
examples: The bank returned the *unsigned* check.
An *unsigned* note was taped to the door.
The contract is still *unsigned*.

senses.gloss: Of a musician or athlete, not under contract with a label or team.
examples: The festival gives a slot to one *unsigned* band each year.
He was *unsigned* until the second week of free agency.

senses.gloss: Impossible to sink, or, of a person, impossible to defeat.
examples: The ship was advertised as *unsinkable*.
This little boat is practically *unsinkable*.
She is the *unsinkable* candidate who survives every scandal.

senses.gloss: Of a person, having no special training for a job.
examples: The factory hired mostly *unskilled* workers.
He arrived in the city young and *unskilled*.

senses.gloss: Of work, needing no special training.
examples: *Unskilled* labor pays less than it used to.
Most of the summer jobs were *unskilled*.

contrast: *Unsociable* only means not fond of company. *Antisocial* is much stronger and means harmful to other people: *antisocial behavior*.

senses.gloss: Not enjoying the company of other people.
examples: He is not rude, just *unsociable* after a long day.
I felt *unsociable* and skipped the party.
Her *unsociable* roommate never came out of her room.

senses.gloss: Still not bought by anyone.
examples: *Unsold* tickets go on sale at half price an hour before the show.
The house sat *unsold* for most of the year.
The store donates *unsold* bread to a shelter.

senses.gloss: Sent or given without being asked for.
examples: My aunt is a rich source of *unsolicited* advice.
The company does not accept *unsolicited* manuscripts.
We get a dozen *unsolicited* emails a day.

contrast: *Unsolvable* means there is no possible answer; *unsolved* means nobody has found the answer yet.

senses.gloss: Impossible to solve.
examples: The puzzle turned out to be *unsolvable*.
Traffic here feels like an *unsolvable* problem.
No problem in this class is *unsolvable*.

senses.gloss: Still without an answer, and in police work still without an arrest.
examples: The case has been *unsolved* since 1978.
The city has dozens of *unsolved* burglaries.
One famous math problem remains *unsolved*.

senses.gloss: Of equipment or methods, simple and basic.
examples: The attack used *unsophisticated* tools that anyone can download.
Their testing was *unsophisticated* but good enough.

senses.gloss: Of a person, having little experience of art, fashion or city life.
examples: He played an *unsophisticated* country lawyer.
I felt *unsophisticated* next to her friends from New York.

contrast: In legal writing *of unsound mind* means not mentally able to make decisions. Outside that phrase, do not use *unsound* about people.

senses.gloss: Of reasoning or a plan, not based on good judgment or good evidence.
examples: The argument is *unsound* because it rests on one bad number.
Economists called the policy financially *unsound*.

senses.gloss: Of a building or structure, not safe or solid.
examples: The inspector found the roof structurally *unsound*.
They tore down the *unsound* porch.

contrast: Two nearly opposite meanings, and only the context tells them apart: *unsparing criticism* is harsh, *unsparing generosity* is large-hearted.

senses.gloss: Holding nothing back in criticism, and so harsh.
examples: The review was *unsparing* about the acting.
She is *unsparing* in her judgment of her own work.

senses.gloss: Giving freely and without limit.
examples: He was *unsparing* with his time when a student needed help.
Their *unsparing* support kept the shelter open.

senses.gloss: Too extreme to describe, almost always about something terrible.
examples: The children suffered *unspeakable* cruelty.
What happened in that village was *unspeakable*.
She lived through *unspeakable* loss and kept working.

contrast: In medicine the usual word is *nonspecific* (*nonspecific symptoms*), and in everyday speech Americans more often say *vague*.

senses.gloss: Not giving details, so it could mean almost anything.
examples: His promises were warm but *unspecific*.
The complaint was so *unspecific* that we could not act on it.
She gave an *unspecific* answer about the date.

senses.gloss: Not named or stated, usually on purpose.
examples: The case was settled for an *unspecified* sum.
He will be away for an *unspecified* period.
The company cited *unspecified* security concerns.

senses.gloss: Solid enough but not impressive or exciting.
examples: He had a long, *unspectacular* career as a backup catcher.
The results were steady and *unspectacular*.
It was an *unspectacular* meal at a fair price.

senses.gloss: Not yet used up, said of money or energy.
examples: *Unspent* funds go back to the state at the end of the year.
He came home with most of his allowance *unspent*.
The boy has a lot of *unspent* energy by bedtime.

contrast: American spelling is *unspoiled*; British books print *unspoilt*.

senses.gloss: Of a place, still beautiful because nothing has been built on it.
examples: They camped on an *unspoiled* stretch of coast.
The valley is one of the last *unspoiled* places in the state.

senses.gloss: Of a person, not made selfish by money or success.
examples: Fame has left her completely *unspoiled*.
The children were polite and *unspoiled*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an unspoken rule*
contrast: An *unspoken* agreement is understood by everyone without being stated. Something *unsaid* was simply never said at all.

senses.gloss: Understood by everyone but never stated out loud.
examples: There is an *unspoken* rule about the parking spots.
They had an *unspoken* agreement never to mention it.
His disappointment stayed *unspoken*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unsportsmanlike conduct*
contrast: *Unsportsmanlike conduct* is the name of the penalty in American football and basketball, so this is the form you hear on TV.

senses.gloss: Not fair or not respectful toward opponents.
senses.ru: неспортивный, некорректный по отношению к сопернику
examples: He was flagged for *unsportsmanlike* conduct.
Taunting the goalie is *unsportsmanlike*.
The coach apologized for his *unsportsmanlike* remarks.

senses.gloss: Not firm, and likely to fall or move.
examples: Do not stand on that ladder, it is *unstable*.
The shelf is *unstable* without the back panel.

senses.gloss: Likely to change suddenly for the worse, said of a situation.
examples: The region has been politically *unstable* for a decade.
Prices are *unstable* this quarter.

senses.gloss: Of a person, having sudden changes of mood or mental state.
examples: The note came from someone clearly *unstable*.
He grew more *unstable* in the months before the arrest.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an unstated assumption*

senses.gloss: Not said directly, though it is part of the thinking.
examples: The plan rests on an *unstated* assumption about growth.
His real reason went *unstated*.
There is an *unstated* rule that juniors answer the phone.

senses.gloss: Not firm on its feet or its base, so it might fall.
examples: She was still *unsteady* on her feet after the surgery.
The table is *unsteady* on this floor.

senses.gloss: Shaking, or not staying at one level.
examples: He poured the coffee with an *unsteady* hand.
Her voice was *unsteady* when she read the letter.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unstinting support*

senses.gloss: Given generously and without holding anything back.
senses.ru: щедрый, не знающий меры (о поддержке, похвале)
examples: Her parents gave *unstinting* support through school.
He was *unstinting* in his praise of the team.
The town offered *unstinting* help to the families.

senses.gloss: Impossible to stop.
examples: In the second half she was *unstoppable*.
The technology now looks *unstoppable*.
They built a seemingly *unstoppable* lead.

senses.gloss: Without a fixed plan, order or organization.
examples: Kids need *unstructured* time to play.
The interview was deliberately *unstructured*.
Most of the data we collect is *unstructured*.

senses.gloss: Not backed up by evidence.
examples: The paper would not print *unsubstantiated* claims.
Two of the three complaints were *unsubstantiated*.
His story remains *unsubstantiated*.

contrast: The *b* is silent, as in *subtle*: *uhn-SUHT-uhl*.

senses.gloss: Obvious and heavy-handed, when something gentler was called for.
examples: He made an *unsubtle* hint about the bill.
The movie has an *unsubtle* message about greed.
Her glance at the clock was distinctly *unsubtle*.

senses.gloss: Not achieving what was wanted.
examples: After an *unsuccessful* first surgery, he tried a different hospital.
She was *unsuccessful* in her run for mayor.
The rescue attempt was *unsuccessful*.

contrast: *Unsuitable* goes comfortably before a noun; *unsuited* almost always follows a verb and takes *to* or *for*.

senses.gloss: Not right for a particular purpose, person or occasion.
examples: The film is *unsuitable* for young children.
She wore shoes that were *unsuitable* for hiking.
They called it an *unsuitable* site for housing.

position: predicative only — *He is unsuited to the job*
contrast: Do not use it before a noun. Say *an unsuitable candidate*, but *The candidate is unsuited to the job*.

senses.gloss: Not having the right qualities for something or someone.
examples: He is *unsuited* to a job with that much travel.
The soil here is *unsuited* for corn.
They were badly *unsuited* to each other.

form: un- + *sung*, from the old sense of songs praising someone
contrast: In practice it appears almost only in *unsung hero* and *unsung heroes*.

senses.gloss: Doing important work that nobody praises.
examples: School nurses are the *unsung* heroes of the district.
He was the *unsung* star of the defense.
The book is about the *unsung* women who ran the lab.

senses.gloss: Without an adult or a manager watching.
examples: Never leave a toddler *unsupervised* near the pool.
*Unsupervised* screen time adds up fast.
The interns were working *unsupervised* all summer.

senses.gloss: Not backed by evidence or facts.
examples: The claim is *unsupported* by any data.
The judge threw out the *unsupported* allegations.

senses.gloss: No longer maintained or made to work, said of software and devices.
examples: That phone runs an *unsupported* version of the operating system.
The browser is *unsupported* after January.

senses.gloss: Not giving encouragement or help to someone who needs it.
examples: Her family was *unsupportive* when she changed careers.
He works for an *unsupportive* manager.
I do not mean to be *unsupportive*, but the numbers worry me.

position: predicative only — *I am unsure*; before a noun use *uncertain*
takes: *about* or *of* + noun; a *wh*-clause (*unsure what to do*); *whether*-clause

senses.gloss: Not certain about a fact or a decision.
examples: I am *unsure* about the date of the meeting.
She was *unsure* whether to take the offer.
He looked *unsure* what to say next.

senses.gloss: Lacking confidence in yourself.
examples: He is still *unsure* of himself in front of a class.
She was shy and *unsure* at fifteen.

position: both — also after the noun: *a record unsurpassed for forty years*

senses.gloss: Better than anything else of its kind.
examples: The view from the ridge is *unsurpassed*.
She had an *unsurpassed* record in the 400 meters.
The shop is *unsurpassed* for repairs of this kind.

contrast: The adverb *unsurprisingly* is even more common and usually opens the sentence: *Unsurprisingly, nobody came*.

senses.gloss: Just what you would expect.
examples: The result was *unsurprising* to anyone who follows the team.
It is *unsurprising* that prices went up.
She gave the *unsurprising* answer that she needed more time.

senses.gloss: Not knowing that something bad is about to happen.
examples: The scam targets *unsuspecting* older customers.
He walked into the room, entirely *unsuspecting*.
They sold the fake tickets to *unsuspecting* fans.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *unsweetened tea*

senses.gloss: With no sugar or sweetener added.
examples: I drink my iced tea *unsweetened*.
The recipe uses *unsweetened* cocoa powder.
Check the label, since most of these brands are not *unsweetened*.

senses.gloss: Never turning aside from a belief, a purpose or a person.
examples: He showed *unswerving* loyalty to his old coach.
Her *unswerving* devotion to the work kept the project alive.
The company has an *unswerving* focus on safety.

contrast: A false friend: English *sympathetic* has nothing to do with Russian *симпатичный*. It means feeling for someone, so *unsympathetic* means cold, not ugly.

senses.gloss: Not feeling or showing pity for someone in trouble.
examples: The doctor was competent but *unsympathetic*.
She gave an *unsympathetic* shrug and went back to work.

senses.gloss: Not in favor of an idea, a group or a plan.
examples: The court has been *unsympathetic* to these arguments.
Management is *unsympathetic* toward the union.

senses.gloss: Not spoiled by something bad that touched everything around it.
examples: He left office *untainted* by the scandal.
The evidence must stay *untainted*.
It was one of the few *untainted* wells in the area.

senses.gloss: Wild, not controlled by people.
examples: The island still has *untamed* forest at its center.
These horses are *untamed*.
He wrote about the *untamed* energy of the city.

senses.gloss: Available but not yet used.
examples: The kid has a lot of *untapped* potential.
Rural areas are an *untapped* market for the service.
The country has *untapped* reserves of natural gas.

senses.gloss: Of a reputation, still clean and respected.
examples: His record is *untarnished* after thirty years on the bench.
Her reputation came through the trial *untarnished*.

senses.gloss: Of metal, still bright and not dull.
examples: The silver was *untarnished* in its lined box.
An *untarnished* brass plate marked the door.

senses.gloss: Not having tax charged on it.
senses.ru: необлагаемый налогом, с которого не уплачен налог
examples: The first part of the benefit is *untaxed*.
The state is losing money to *untaxed* online sales.
He kept the tips *untaxed* and off the books.

senses.gloss: Impossible to defend or to keep going.
examples: His position on the board became *untenable*.
That argument is *untenable* once you read the data.
Rising rents made staying in the city *untenable*.

senses.gloss: Not yet tried out, so nobody knows if it works.
examples: The treatment is promising but *untested* in humans.
Thousands of kits sat *untested* in storage.

senses.gloss: Of a person, not yet proven in a difficult situation.
examples: The team is starting an *untested* quarterback.
She is smart but *untested* in a crisis.

form: un- + *tethered*, from *tether* (a rope that holds an animal)

senses.gloss: No longer tied to anything, in fact or in a figure of speech.
examples: An *untethered* balloon drifted over the field.
Stock prices seem *untethered* from company earnings.
After the layoff he felt completely *untethered*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *It was unthinkable*
takes: *that*-clause (*unthinkable that she would lie*); *to*-infinitive (*unthinkable to refuse*)

senses.gloss: So shocking or extreme that you cannot imagine it happening.
examples: Twenty years ago this would have been *unthinkable*.
It is *unthinkable* that they would close the hospital.
The war forced families into *unthinkable* choices.

senses.gloss: Not frightening or dangerous, and easy to be around.
examples: He has a quiet, *unthreatening* manner with patients.
The dog looked big but *unthreatening*.
They wanted a mascot that was friendly and *unthreatening*.

contrast: Americans usually say *messy* about a room and *unkempt* about a person; *untidy* sounds a little formal or British.

senses.gloss: Not neat; with things left out of place.
examples: His desk is permanently *untidy*.
She came in with *untidy* hair and muddy boots.
The garage got *untidier* every weekend.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *your shoelace is untied*
contrast: Watch the spelling: *untied* (not tied) is one letter away from *united*.

senses.gloss: With the knot loose or undone.
examples: Your shoelace is *untied*.
He walked around all day with an *untied* apron.
The boat was left *untied* at the dock.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *his untimely death*
contrast: It ends in *-ly* but it is an adjective, not an adverb. Say *The remark came at an untimely moment*, not *He spoke untimely*.

senses.gloss: Happening far too early, especially of a death.
examples: The article marked the tenth year since his *untimely* death.
An *untimely* frost ruined the crop.

senses.gloss: Coming at a bad moment.
examples: Her joke was *untimely*, to say the least.
The report landed at an *untimely* point in the campaign.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *untiring efforts*

senses.gloss: Working on and on without getting tired or giving up.
examples: We thanked the volunteers for their *untiring* work.
She was *untiring* in her support of the library.
He is an *untiring* advocate for these families.

senses.gloss: Having no title or name.
examples: The gallery is showing an *untitled* painting from 1962.
He is working on an as yet *untitled* album.
The album is still *untitled*.

senses.gloss: Too great to be counted or measured.
examples: The storm did *untold* damage to the coast.
The family had *untold* wealth.

senses.gloss: Never told to anyone.
examples: The film covers the *untold* story of the first crew.
Her side of it remains the *untold* part.

senses.gloss: Safe from punishment, criticism or being fired.
examples: For years the coach was *untouchable* at that school.
The program is politically *untouchable*.
Nobody in this company is *untouchable*.

senses.gloss: So good that no one can match it.
examples: On clay she was simply *untouchable*.
They built an *untouchable* lead by halftime.

senses.gloss: Not handled, eaten or used.
examples: She left her dinner *untouched*.
The money sat *untouched* in the account for years.
She sent back an *untouched* plate of pasta.

senses.gloss: Not affected by something that changed everything around it.
examples: Two blocks were *untouched* by the fire.
No family in the town was left *untouched* by the closing.

position: attributive only — also after *nothing*, *anything* or *something*: *nothing untoward*
contrast: Formal and slightly old-fashioned. Americans say it in two syllables, *uhn-TORD*, and most often in the phrase *nothing untoward*.

senses.gloss: Unexpected and unwelcome, though usually not serious.
examples: The nurse reported nothing *untoward* overnight.
The drug caused no *untoward* effects.
Neighbors noticed nothing *untoward* about the house.

senses.gloss: Impossible to follow back to its source or owner.
examples: The payment was made in *untraceable* cash.
He called from an *untraceable* number.
The poison is virtually *untraceable*.

contrast: *To the untrained eye* is a fixed phrase meaning to someone without expert knowledge.

senses.gloss: Not taught the skills a job or task needs.
examples: *Untrained* staff were left to run the shift.
To the *untrained* eye the two paintings look identical.
The dog is friendly but completely *untrained*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to put into another language without losing the meaning.
examples: The pun is *untranslatable*.
She says the word is *untranslatable* into English.
Some jokes are nearly *untranslatable*.

senses.gloss: Not given medical care.
examples: *Untreated* high blood pressure damages the heart.
The infection went *untreated* for weeks.

senses.gloss: Not put through a chemical or industrial process.
examples: *Untreated* sewage was running into the river.
The deck is built from *untreated* pine.

senses.gloss: Calm, and not worried by anything.
examples: He seemed *untroubled* by the criticism.
She had an *untroubled* childhood on the coast.
The lake was flat and *untroubled* at dawn.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *That is untrue*
takes: *to* + person for the second sense (*untrue to his wife*)
contrast: Before a noun Americans usually say *false* or *a false claim* rather than *an untrue claim*.

senses.gloss: Not true; not matching the facts.
examples: The rumor is completely *untrue*.
The form warns against making *untrue* statements.
It is simply *untrue* that we were warned.

senses.gloss: Not faithful or loyal to someone.
examples: He had been *untrue* to her for years.
She refused to be *untrue* to her own principles.

senses.gloss: Not to be trusted, whether a person or a source of information.
examples: Voters found both candidates *untrustworthy*.
The site is an *untrustworthy* source for medical advice.
He proved *untrustworthy* with money.

contrast: A softer, more formal way of saying that someone lied: *He was untruthful about his hours*.

senses.gloss: Not telling the truth, or not true.
examples: He was *untruthful* about where he had been.
The application contained *untruthful* statements.
I do not think she is being *untruthful*, just careless.
